stem: A 68-year-old man presents with painful inability to pass urine. He is haemodynamically stable and has a palpable distended bladder. What is the immediate priority?

options.text: Prompt bladder decompression with an appropriate urinary catheter, after checking for contraindications to urethral catheterization
Start an antimuscarinic and review in one week
Perform cystoscopy before relieving the retention

explanation: Acute painful urinary retention requires prompt assessment and bladder decompression. Check for urethral injury or other contraindications; if urethral catheterization is unsuccessful or inappropriate, seek urgent urological help for an alternative drainage route. Investigate the cause after stabilization.
source_title: NICE guideline CG97: Lower urinary tract symptoms in men

stem: A newborn boy has poor urinary stream, bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, and a thick-walled bladder. Which diagnosis should be urgently considered?
explanation: Posterior urethral valves are an important cause of congenital bladder outlet obstruction in boys. Prompt pediatric urology assessment is required to protect renal function; evaluation and management depend on clinical status and imaging.
source_title: PubMed literature search: posterior urethral valves

stem: A patient with diabetes has a non-compressible ankle artery and an unexpectedly high ankle-brachial index despite clinical concern for peripheral arterial disease. What best explains this?

options.text: Medial arterial calcification causing falsely elevated ankle pressure
A normal ABI excludes arterial disease

explanation: Medial arterial calcification can make ankle arteries poorly compressible and produce a falsely high ABI. Consider toe pressures or toe-brachial index and interpret results alongside symptoms and examination.
source_title: NICE guideline CG147: Peripheral arterial disease
